headline: YOUR NEWSPAPER WILL TALK TO YOU
deck: A story set in 2889 imagines the daily paper read aloud to 85 million subscribers, and recorded for later.
quote: Instead of being printed, the Earth Chronicle is every morning spoken to subscribers, who, in interesting conversations with reporters, statesmen, and scientists, learn the news of the day.
quote_note: From a short story. Published under Jules Verne's name; Project Gutenberg notes it is now thought to be chiefly the work of his son, Michel Verne.

quote_sources.title: In the Year 2889 — Project Gutenberg

happened: Spoken news on demand is ordinary now. Pew Research found roughly half of US adults had listened to a podcast in the past year (2023).

happened_sources.title: Podcasts as a source of news and information — Pew Research Center, 18 Apr 2023

reason: Set in 2889, but spoken, recorded news arrived about 870 years early.

headline: SUBMARINES WILL ONLY SUFFOCATE THEIR CREWS
deck: The great forecaster of the age cannot picture the submarine doing anything useful.
quote: I must confess that my imagination, in spite even of spurring, refuses to see any sort of submarine doing anything but suffocate its crew and founder at sea.

quote_sources.title: Anticipations, by H. G. Wells — Project Gutenberg eBook #19229

happened: In 1958 the nuclear submarine USS Nautilus crossed under the North Pole, fully submerged, and her crew came home to a Presidential Unit Citation.

happened_sources.title: Nautilus (SSN-571) — Naval History and Heritage Command

reason: Submarines became some of the most capable ships ever built.

headline: FLYING MACHINE MAY TAKE TEN MILLION YEARS
deck: A newspaper editorial says a machine that really flies is a very long way off.
quote: ...it might be assumed that the flying machine which will really fly might be evolved by the combined and continuous efforts of mathematicians and mechanics in from one million to ten million years...

quote_sources.title: The New York Times, 9 Oct 1903, "Flying Machines Which Do Not Fly" — Wikisource transcription
Snopes fact check

happened: Sixty-nine days later, on 17 December 1903, the Wright brothers flew the first powered, controlled aeroplane.

happened_sources.title: 1903 Wright Flyer — Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

reason: Out by about ten million years, minus 69 days.

headline: A NEWSPAPER YOU HEAR, NOT READ
deck: An inventor's nightly broadcasts to amateur operators around New York are billed as the start of something new.
quote: ...it foretells, according to the inventor of the audion lamp, the coming of the worlds first regular spoken, or wireless telephone newspaper.
quote_note: Reported speech: the trade paper Telephony paraphrasing Lee de Forest. "worlds" is spelled as in the transcription.
who: Lee de Forest, as reported by Telephony

quote_sources.title: "Wireless Telephone Newspaper", Telephony, 30 Dec 1916 — Early Radio History transcription

happened: By 1921 the Westinghouse station in Pittsburgh was sending out nightly programmes of music and "national and international news". Radio news became an everyday thing.

happened_sources.title: "A New Era in Wireless" (1921) on KDKA — Early Radio History transcription

reason: The spoken newspaper arrived within five years and never left.

headline: PUT THE SUN TO WORK ON YOUR ROOF
deck: The telephone's inventor looks at the flat roofs of Washington and sees wasted power.
quote: What wide expanses of roof are available in all our large cities for the utilization of the sun's rays!
quote_note: Bell pictured pipes of oil heated by the sun, not solar panels. He also wrote: "We can take coal out of a mine, but we can never put it back."
where: "Prizes for the Inventor", National Geographic Magazine

quote_sources.title: National Geographic Magazine, Feb 1917, "Prizes for the Inventor" — Wikisource transcription

happened: Rooftops and fields now carry solar panels by the million. The energy think tank Ember says solar generation grew faster than ever in the first half of 2025, breaking a new record.

happened_sources.title: Global Electricity Mid-Year Insights 2025 — Ember, 7 Oct 2025

reason: Different kit, same idea: the roof became a power station.

headline: STAY IN TOUCH WHEREVER YOU WANDER
deck: A radio engineer's textbook imagines receivers so light that nobody need ever be out of reach.
quote: So that it should become ultimately possible to keep in immediate touch with the traveling individual regardless of his motion or temporary location.

quote_sources.title: Alfred N. Goldsmith, Radio Telephony (1918), extract — Early Radio History

happened: The ITU says four out of five people aged 10 or older now own a mobile phone.

happened_sources.title: Facts and Figures 2024: Mobile phone ownership — ITU

reason: Your pocket proves it every time it buzzes.

headline: A ROCKET COULD REACH THE MOON, SAYS PROFESSOR
deck: A quiet physics paper works out how much flash powder a rocket would need to be seen hitting the Moon.
quote: His 1919 treatise, "A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes", showed that a rocket, if developed and built in stages, was theoretically capable of a flight to the Moon.
quote_note: In our words, following the Smithsonian's description. The original paper is a scanned PDF we could not read as text, so no direct quotation is used.
where: "A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes", Smithsonian Institution

quote_sources.title: Box, magnesium powder experiment, R.H. Goddard — Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

happened: Fifty years later a staged rocket carried Apollo 11 to the Moon, landing on 20 July 1969.

happened_sources.title: Apollo 11 mission overview — NASA

reason: The maths was right; it just needed half a century of engineering.

headline: EDISON SEEKS A TELEPHONE TO THE DEAD
deck: The great inventor says he is working on an apparatus to reach those who have died.
quote: To see if it is possible for personalities which have left this earth to communicate with us.

quote_sources.title: Edison and science fiction — Thomas Edison Papers, Rutgers
Edison's Views on Life and Death — Scientific American, 30 Oct 1920

happened: Edison's archive at Rutgers says no verifiable evidence of such a device has ever been found.

happened_sources.title: Edison and science fiction — Thomas Edison Papers, Rutgers

reason: As ruled on air in the Halloween Short.

headline: ROCKETS CANNOT WORK IN A VACUUM, PAPER SCOFFS
deck: An editorial mocks Professor Goddard's plan to reach space and says he lacks high-school science.
quote: Of course, he only seems to lack the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools.
quote_note: The editorial argued a rocket needs "something better than a vacuum against which to react". It is a claim more than a forecast, but it was a claim about what rockets would never do.

quote_sources.title: FAQs about Robert H. Goddard — Clark University Archives (archived copy)

happened: On 17 July 1969, three days before the Moon walk, the Times printed: "it is now definitely established that a rocket can function in a vacuum as well as in an atmosphere. The Times regrets the error."

happened_sources.title: FAQs about Robert H. Goddard — Clark University Archives (archived copy)

reason: The paper corrected itself, 49 years later.

headline: THE DAY'S NEWS, WHILE IT IS STILL HAPPENING
deck: An official proposes a free government radio news service for anyone with a $65 receiver.
quote: ...to put the day's news into the hands of all who wish it while it is still happening.
quote_note: Part of a stated aim for a proposed service, quoted in a newspaper report.

quote_sources.title: "Radio Newspaper" proposal, Brownwood Bulletin, 23 Aug 1921 — Early Radio History transcription

happened: Live news is now in almost every pocket. Pew Research says an overwhelming majority of US adults at least sometimes get news from digital devices.

happened_sources.title: News Platform Fact Sheet — Pew Research Center

reason: "While it is still happening" is now the whole business model.

headline: ONE DAY WE'LL CALCULATE THE WEATHER FASTER THAN IT ARRIVES
deck: A scientist spends years forecasting six hours of weather by hand, and calls the real thing a dream.
quote: Perhaps some day in the dim future it will be possible to advance the computations faster than the weather advances and at a cost less than the saving to mankind due to the information gained. But that is a dream.
quote_note: From the preface, as quoted by meteorologist Peter Lynch.

quote_sources.title: Peter Lynch, The Emergence of Numerical Weather Prediction, Chapter 1 (PDF) — University College Dublin

happened: Weather forecasts are now run routinely on powerful computers using methods remarkably like Richardson's.

happened_sources.title: Peter Lynch, Chapter 1 (PDF) — University College Dublin

reason: The dream runs every few hours on a supercomputer.

headline: ROWS OF METAL WINDMILLS WILL POWER BRITAIN
deck: A young biologist tells Cambridge students how the country will be powered in 400 years.
quote: The country will be covered with rows of metallic windmills working electric motors which in their turn supply current at a very high voltage to great electric mains.
quote_note: He was forecasting "four hundred years hence". He also pictured storing surplus wind power as hydrogen.
where: "Daedalus, or Science and the Future" (lecture, later a book)

quote_sources.title: Daedalus, or Science and the Future — Project Gutenberg eBook #70955

happened: Wind farms are a common sight now. Ember says solar and wind together outpaced the growth in world electricity demand in the first half of 2025.

happened_sources.title: Global Electricity Mid-Year Insights 2025 — Ember, 7 Oct 2025

reason: He gave it 400 years. It took about 100.

headline: A BOMB THE SIZE OF AN ORANGE COULD LEVEL A TOWN
deck: A future prime minister asks whether science has really finished inventing explosives.
quote: Might not a bomb no bigger than an orange be found to possess a secret power to destroy a whole block of buildings—nay to concentrate the force of a thousand tons of cordite and blast a township at a stroke?
quote_note: Posed as a question, in an essay warning about future war.
where: "Shall We All Commit Suicide?", Nash's Pall Mall Magazine

quote_sources.title: "Shall We All Commit Suicide?" — International Churchill Society, Finest Hour 94
Churchill's scientific imagination — Hillsdale College Churchill Project

happened: On 6 August 1945 a single atomic bomb destroyed most of Hiroshima.

happened_sources.title: The Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima, August 6, 1945 — US Department of Energy, Manhattan Project history

reason: A grim one to get right, 21 years early.

headline: MUSIC AT THE TOUCH OF A BUTTON BY 2024
deck: A newspaper looks a hundred years ahead and hears grand homes filling with music on demand.
quote: A hundred years from now the salons of the magnificent private houses will be flooded by the touch of a button with divine tones.
quote_note: As quoted by Paleofuture from a 1924 newspaper article attributed to R. M. Kerr.

quote_sources.title: Future musicians may not even have to leave their homes, according to 1924 — Paleofuture

happened: 752 million people paid for a music streaming subscription in 2024, says the record industry body IFPI. And you don't need a salon.

happened_sources.title: IFPI Global Music Report 2025 press release

reason: Right on the year, and it reached far more than the magnificent houses.

headline: YOUR DOCTOR WILL "FEEL" YOU FROM MILES AWAY
deck: A magazine editor sketches robot arms that let a doctor examine a patient from far away.
quote: The Teledactyl (Tele, far; Dactyl, finger — from the Greek) is a future instrument by which it will be possible for us to "feel at a distance."
quote_note: As quoted by Smithsonian magazine; Gernsback set the device in 1975.

quote_sources.title: Telemedicine Predicted in 1925 — Smithsonian Magazine (Paleofuture)

happened: Smithsonian magazine said in 2012 that Gernsback "effectively predicted telemedicine", but that a home device for touching patients at a distance still did not exist.

happened_sources.title: Telemedicine Predicted in 1925 — Smithsonian Magazine (Paleofuture)

reason: Remote doctors: yes. Robot fingers on the bedside table: not so much.

headline: TELEVISION'S FUTURE: NEWS AS IT HAPPENS
deck: The phone company is doubtful television will ever pay. A newspaper is not so sure.
quote: The commercial future of television, if it has one, is thought to be largely in public entertainment — super-news reels flashed before audiences at the moment of occurrence...
quote_note: Shortened with "..."; quoted by the paper's own Times Insider feature in 2015.
where: Report on the first long-distance television demonstration

quote_sources.title: 1927: "Commercial Use in Doubt," The Times Said About Television — NYT Times Insider, 12 Feb 2015

happened: In 1969 an estimated 650 million people watched live television pictures of Neil Armstrong on the Moon.

happened_sources.title: Apollo 11 mission overview — NASA

reason: "If it has one" turned into the biggest live audience in history at the time.

headline: AMERICA ON THE BRINK OF ENDING POVERTY
deck: Accepting his party's nomination, the next president says the poorhouse is vanishing.
quote: We in America today are nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land.
where: Speech accepting the Republican nomination, Stanford, California

quote_sources.title: Address Accepting the Republican Presidential Nomination — The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara

happened: The stock market crashed the next year. By the summer of 1932 the Dow was 89 percent below its peak, in the depths of the Great Depression.

happened_sources.title: Stock Market Crash of 1929 — Federal Reserve History

reason: The timing could hardly have been worse.

headline: FLYING ABROAD WILL BE AN EVERYDAY AFFAIR
deck: A British car maker pictures the world of the future and puts holidaymakers in the sky.
quote: Journeys to foreign countries by air will be a matter of everyday occurrence...
quote_note: As quoted by Paleofuture. Sir Herbert Austin added it would need "a universal language" to really take off.

quote_sources.title: Electric cars are the future, according to this British auto exec from 1928 — Paleofuture

happened: Flying abroad is routine for millions. Paleofuture notes Austin was "spot-on" about air travel.

happened_sources.title: Paleofuture on Sir Herbert Austin, 1928

reason: The universal language never arrived; the flights did.

headline: STOCKS HAVE REACHED A PERMANENT HIGH, SAYS YALE MAN
deck: The nation's best-known economist tells a dinner audience the boom is here to stay.
quote: Stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau.
quote_note: As reported by The New York Times, 16 Oct 1929, p. 8.
where: Speech to the Purchasing Agents Association, New York

quote_sources.title: Stock Market Crash of 1929 — Federal Reserve History

happened: Within two weeks came Black Monday and Black Tuesday. By mid-1932 the Dow was 89% below its peak, and it did not get back there until November 1954.

happened_sources.title: Stock Market Crash of 1929 — Federal Reserve History

reason: The plateau lasted about nine days.

headline: THE WORST IS OVER, PRESIDENT ASSURES BUSINESS
deck: Six months after the crash, the White House tells business leaders recovery is near.
quote: While the crash only took place 6 months ago, I am convinced we have now passed the worst and with continued unity of effort we shall rapidly recover.
where: Address to the US Chamber of Commerce

quote_sources.title: Address to the Chamber of Commerce of the United States, 1 May 1930 — The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara

happened: The slide went on until the summer of 1932, when the Dow hit its lowest close of the century. It didn't get back to its 1929 peak until November 1954.

happened_sources.title: Stock Market Crash of 1929 — Federal Reserve History

reason: The worst still had two years to run.

headline: ATOM POWER IS "MOONSHINE", SAYS RUTHERFORD
deck: The father of nuclear physics tells scientists not to expect energy from splitting atoms.
quote: Anyone who expects a source of power from the transformation of these atoms is talking moonshine.
quote_note: Reported in the press after his British Association speech. Newspapers printed slightly different wordings; Quote Investigator lists them.
where: British Association for the Advancement of Science, Leicester

quote_sources.title: Quote Investigator: "Talking moonshine"

happened: Nine years later, on 2 December 1942, the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction ran under a Chicago football stadium.

happened_sources.title: 10 intriguing facts about the world's first nuclear chain reaction — US Department of Energy

reason: The moonshine was flowing within a decade.

headline: YOUR MORNING PAPER, ON A SCREEN
deck: A newspaper cartoon asks whether the front page could one day be sent to your television.
quote: Some day you may be able to receive the front page of your morning newspaper this way—fully printed and shown on the screen of a television set. Can it be done?
quote_note: From Ray Gross's syndicated panel "Can It Be Done?", as quoted by Paleofuture (Marion Progress, North Carolina, 29 Mar 1934).

quote_sources.title: This "Television Newspaper" was predicted decades before TV went mainstream — Paleofuture

happened: An overwhelming majority of US adults now at least sometimes get their news on digital screens, says Pew Research.

happened_sources.title: News Platform Fact Sheet — Pew Research Center

reason: It can be done. You may be doing it now.

headline: A TELEVISION IN EVERY HOME WITHIN THREE YEARS
deck: A television company engineer tells a Rotary club the sets are nearly here for everyone.
quote: in practically every home within three years.
quote_note: The words reported by The News; quoted by TV historian John Wyver.
who: Captain A. G. D. West, Baird Television
where: The News, report of a Rotary Club talk

quote_sources.title: On this day in early British television: 8 February 1935 — Illuminations (John Wyver)

happened: When the BBC switched television off for the war on 1 September 1939, only about 20,000 households had sets.

happened_sources.title: Close down of television service for the duration of the war — BBC History

reason: Practically every home turned out to be about 20,000 of them.

headline: LANDON TO WIN THE WHITE HOUSE, BIG POLL SAYS
deck: A magazine mails ten million ballots and is confident it knows the next president.
quote: Based on its poll of about 2.3 million returned postcards, The Literary Digest predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt with 57.1% of the popular vote and 370 electoral votes.
quote_note: In our words, from a university statistics page. We did not find the magazine's own wording online.

quote_sources.title: The Literary Digest Poll — Random (Probability, Mathematical Statistics, Stochastic Processes), University of Alabama in Huntsville

happened: Roosevelt won with 60.8% of the vote and an electoral landslide of 523 to 8.

happened_sources.title: The Literary Digest Poll — randomservices.org

reason: Ten million postcards, one very wrong answer.

headline: ALL HUMAN KNOWLEDGE, OPEN TO EVERYONE
deck: A famous novelist proposes a "world brain" and says it may come soon.
quote: The whole human memory can be, and probably in a short time will be, made accessible to every individual.
quote_note: He imagined it on microfilm.

quote_sources.title: World Brain, by H. G. Wells — Project Gutenberg Australia

happened: In 2024, 5.5 billion people were online, 68 per cent of the world, says the ITU.

happened_sources.title: Facts and Figures 2024: Internet use — ITU

reason: Not microfilm, but the world brain is open most hours of the day.

headline: "PEACE FOR OUR TIME", SAYS PRIME MINISTER
deck: Back from Munich, Britain's leader tells the crowd to go home and sleep soundly.
quote: I believe it is peace for our time... Go home and get a nice quiet sleep.

quote_sources.title: Neville Chamberlain's "Peace For Our Time" speech — EuroDocs, Brigham Young University
Chamberlain's "Peace for Our Time" speech — US Holocaust Memorial Museum

happened: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, starting World War II. Britain declared war two days later.

happened_sources.title: Invasion of Poland, Fall 1939 — US Holocaust Memorial Museum

reason: Our time lasted eleven months.

headline: SCIENTIST WARNS PRESIDENT OF A NEW KIND OF BOMB
deck: A letter to Roosevelt says uranium could be used to build bombs of terrible power.
quote: This new phenomenon would also lead to the construction of bombs, and it is conceivable--though much less certain--that extremely powerful bombs of this type may thus be constructed.
quote_note: The same letter guessed such bombs "might very well prove too heavy for transportation by air". That part was wrong.
who: Albert Einstein (letter drafted with Leo Szilard)
where: Letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt

quote_sources.title: Einstein's Letter to Franklin D. Roosevelt — Atomic Archive

happened: Six years later, on 6 August 1945, an atomic bomb dropped from a plane destroyed Hiroshima.

happened_sources.title: The Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima, August 6, 1945 — US Department of Energy

reason: "Much less certain" became certain far too quickly.

headline: FORD: THE FLYING CAR IS COMING
deck: The motor king says a combination airplane and motor car is on its way.
quote: Mark my word: A combination airplane and motor car is coming.

quote_sources.title: Henry Ford quotations — The Henry Ford

happened: Klein Vision's AirCar received a certificate of airworthiness in January 2022. It is a roadable aircraft.

happened_sources.title: AirCar receives certificate of airworthiness — The Engineer

reason: As ruled on air in Episode 1.

headline: WATCH THE 2033 ECLIPSE FROM THE MOON
deck: A Sunday magazine books the best seat for an eclipse 92 years away.
quote: If scientists of 2033 do reach the moon properly equipped they will see the sun totally eclipsed by the earth from 1:07 to 3:43 p.m. on April 14th.
quote_note: Written by Schlesinger in The American Weekly; as quoted by Paleofuture.

quote_sources.title: Scientists of 1941 predicted we'd be watching the eclipse from the Moon — Paleofuture

happened: In April 2026 NASA's Artemis II crew flew around the Moon and back. Nobody has landed there since 1972, and 2033 is still to come.

happened_sources.title: NASA welcomes record-setting Artemis II Moonfarers back to Earth — NASA

reason: Seven years to go. Pack a folding chair.

headline: COMMUTE BY HELICOPTER FROM YOUR OFFICE TERRACE
deck: A whisky advert promises the man who plans ahead his own aircraft after the war.
quote: Step from your office building terrace into your Helicopter and commute to your hunting lodge on a mountain lake 200 miles away! That's more than a commuter's dream, for the Helicopters already designed will make it possible for you Tomorrow!
quote_note: Advert copy in Life magazine, as quoted by Paleofuture.

quote_sources.title: Seagram promised whiskey drinkers their own commuter helicopter in 1943 — Paleofuture

happened: Helicopters are real, but as Paleofuture puts it, "we're still waiting on personal helicopters to go mainstream".

happened_sources.title: Paleofuture on the 1943 Seagram advert

reason: The office terrace is still for smokers, not pilots.

headline: A HELICOPTER BEHIND THE APPLE TREE
deck: A science magazine pictures suburban commuters whizzing to the office roof.
quote: A helicopter in your back yard? The picture is bright. You go out behind the apple tree, give the rotors a whirl, and whizz!—you're on the office roof.
quote_note: As quoted by Paleofuture. The magazine added you would have to keep the machine in perfect condition.

quote_sources.title: The 1940s promised helicopters in every American's backyard — Paleofuture

happened: Eighty years on, ordinary commuters still don't keep a helicopter out back. Paleofuture: "we're still waiting on personal helicopters to go mainstream".

happened_sources.title: Paleofuture on the 1943 Seagram advert

reason: The delphiniums are fine. The rotors never came.

headline: RADIO STATIONS IN SPACE COULD COVER THE WHOLE WORLD
deck: A young engineer works out that a station 42,000 km out would hang still in the sky.
quote: A true broadcast service, giving constant field strength at all times over the whole globe would be invaluable, not to say indispensable, in a world society.
quote_note: The article shows that a body in an orbit with a radius of 42,000 km takes exactly 24 hours to go round, and so stays above the same spot.

quote_sources.title: Extra-Terrestrial Relays (Wireless World, Oct 1945) — transcription, pages 305–308
Extra-Terrestrial Relays — facsimile PDF (Universidad de los Andes space-law archive)

happened: In 1964 the geostationary satellite Syncom 3 carried TV pictures of the Tokyo Olympics to the United States. Geostationary satellites still carry the bulk of space-based communications.

happened_sources.title: Communications Satellite, Syncom — Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

reason: The orbit he described is still used for satellite TV and weather satellites.

headline: THOUSANDS OF HELICOPTERS ON EVERYDAY ERRANDS
deck: A young inventor advertises for investors to build the commuter helicopter.
quote: Thousands of helicopters cruising soon over cities and towns and open country on dozens of kinds of errands.
quote_note: From a newspaper advert by Stanley Hiller Jr., as quoted by Paleofuture.

quote_sources.title: The 1940s promised helicopters in every American's backyard — Paleofuture

happened: Helicopters do run all kinds of errands now (rescue, news, hospitals, oil rigs), but the mass commuter helicopter never took off.

happened_sources.title: Paleofuture on 1940s helicopter predictions

reason: Thousands of errands, yes. Your errands, no.

headline: TINY NEW DEVICE MAY CHANGE ELECTRONICS
deck: A phone company lab shows off a gadget smaller than a fingertip that can do a vacuum tube's job.
quote: Although the device is still in the laboratory stage, Bell scientists and engineers expect it may have far-reaching significance in electronics and electrical communication.

quote_sources.title: Bell Labs transistor announcement press release, 1948 (PDF) — Bell System Memorial

happened: Single chips now hold billions of transistors, says the Computer History Museum.

happened_sources.title: 1965: Moore's Law predicts the future of integrated circuits — Computer History Museum

reason: Possibly the biggest understatement ever put in a press release.

headline: COMPUTERS MAY ONE DAY WEIGH ONLY 1½ TONS
deck: A science magazine imagines the giant electronic brains slimming down.
quote: Where a calculator like the ENIAC today is equipped with 18,000 vacuum tubes and weighs 30 tons, computers in the future may have only 1,000 vacuum tubes and perhaps weigh only 1 1/2 tons.

quote_sources.title: "A Virtual Space Odyssey; This Time, the Future Is Closer Than You Think" — The New York Times, 31 Dec 2000

happened: Laptops and desktop PCs, each vastly more powerful than ENIAC, were everywhere by 2000, as the Times noted. Today a phone in your pocket outruns it.

happened_sources.title: The New York Times, 31 Dec 2000

reason: Right that computers would shrink; wrong by roughly a factor of a thousand on how much.

headline: MACHINES WILL PASS FOR HUMAN WITHIN 50 YEARS
deck: A Manchester mathematician proposes a test: can a judge tell a computer from a person?
quote: I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible, to programme computers... to make them play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning.
quote_note: Shortened with "..." (it gives a storage size).

quote_sources.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence (Mind, 1950) — PDF, UMBC course archive

happened: In a 2025 study with five-minute chats, people picked the AI model GPT-4.5 as the human 73% of the time.

happened_sources.title: Jones & Bergen, "Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test" — arXiv 2503.23674 (2025)

reason: It happened, about 25 years after his "fifty years".

headline: THE WOMAN OF 2000 WILL CARRY HER OWN TELEPHONE
deck: Fashion experts sketch an Easter outfit for the year 2000, accessories included.
quote: They say women will tote their own food, fuel and telephones in mesh bags.
quote_note: Caption from the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin, crediting "Chicago fashion experts"; as quoted by Paleofuture.

quote_sources.title: Mama's Easter parade costume of 2000 A.D. (1951) — Paleofuture

happened: Four out of five people aged 10 or older now own a mobile phone, says the ITU. The mesh bag is optional.

happened_sources.title: Facts and Figures 2024: Mobile phone ownership — ITU

reason: The phone and the snacks, yes. Carrying your own fuel, thankfully not.

headline: A SPACE STATION IS "INEVITABLE AS THE RISING OF THE SUN"
deck: Wernher von Braun shows the nation a wheel-shaped station orbiting the Earth.
quote: ...as "inevitable as the rising of the sun."
quote_note: Paraphrase plus a short quoted phrase: von Braun predicted that the development of a space station orbiting Earth was as "inevitable as the rising of the sun" (New York Times TierneyLab, 2008).

quote_sources.title: Von Braun's Spaceship — The New York Times (TierneyLab), 14 Oct 2008
Von Braun, "Crossing the Last Frontier," Collier's, 22 Mar 1952 — University of Oregon digital exhibit

happened: People have lived on the International Space Station continuously since 2 November 2000.

happened_sources.title: International Space Station — NASA

reason: The station came; it is more of a laboratory than his wheel.

headline: THE SECRET OF HOW LIFE COPIES ITSELF?
deck: Two young scientists describe the shape of DNA, and drop a very big hint in one sentence.
quote: It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.

quote_sources.title: Watson & Crick, "Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids", Nature, 25 Apr 1953 (PDF) — National Human Genome Research Institute

happened: The base-pairing copying idea was confirmed, and in 1962 Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins won the Nobel Prize for their discoveries about the molecular structure of nucleic acids.

happened_sources.title: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1962 — NobelPrize.org

reason: The most modest-sounding sentence in modern science.

headline: SPACE TRAVEL IS "UTTER BILGE", SAYS ASTRONOMER ROYAL
deck: Britain's top astronomer dismisses the whole idea of going into space.
quote: ...as late as 1956, Britain's Astronomer Royal called the prospect of space travel "utter bilge."
quote_note: Paraphrase with a two-word quote, as reported by Time magazine in 1966. Time does not name him; the Astronomer Royal in 1956 was Sir Richard Woolley.

quote_sources.title: "The Futurists: Looking Toward A.D. 2000" — Time, 25 Feb 1966

happened: The next year, on 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.

happened_sources.title: Sputnik and the Dawn of the Space Age — NASA History (archived copy)

reason: Space travel began about a year later.

headline: TELEVISION THAT HANGS ON THE WALL
deck: An aircraft company's magazine advert promises flat screens thanks to its tiny transistors.
quote: How soon can you enjoy on-the-wall television? Chances are, it will be here in a relatively short time.
quote_note: Advert copy from Hughes Aircraft in Newsweek, as quoted by Paleofuture.

quote_sources.title: CCTV and shipping via missile: 7 ideas for the future from a 1950s tech company — Paleofuture

happened: Flat-screen TVs in the home did come true, says Paleofuture. They became common around the 2000s, nearly half a century later.
